description: Soy Maximiliano Maidana, creador e impulsor del Proyecto CENTRE. Me apasiona la innovación tecnológica, el desarrollo de energías renovables y la búsqueda de soluciones disruptivas para los desafíos de la exploración espacial y la sostenibilidad en la Tierra
summary: It is an interactive, browser-based educational simulator designed for children aged 7 to 12 to experience the real engineering trade-offs behind deep-space survival. We developed a voice-guided, gamified platform that integrates a Space Academy, a 3D Electronic Dough Tactile Matrix (60×60 channels) for molding rover bridges and radiation-shielding regolith walls, a Habitat Workshop where every upgrade carries a real energy cost, a Sol-by-Sol Survival Simulation, and an Orbital Docking Simulator. The project tackles the challenge by grounding every decision in real data from NASA DONKI (solar flares), RadLab (radiation doses), OSDR (space biology), Mars Trek/LRO (real topography), and nutritional guidelines from the Canadian Space Agency (CSA). It matters because it transforms abstract space concepts into tangible decisions without technical barriers—allowing young learners to understand how to balance power, oxygen, and shielding just like real NASA mission planners.
details:
Centre is an interactive, browser-based educational platform designed under the clean network protocol concept edu:// so that children and youth aged 7 to 12 (alongside teachers and families) can manage an outpost on the Moon and Mars, tangibly experiencing the real engineering trade-offs behind deep-space survival.

The tool runs directly on the web with no downloads, ads, or prior registration required, guiding users through 5 interactive modules narrated in Argentine Spanish:

  • edu:// Space Academy (Sphere 1): 5 educational sectors featuring audio and trivia covering 70° Zigzag solar harvesting (measured in qums), battery banks for the 14-day lunar night, 3D regolith shielding, hydroponic farming (CSA), and safe browsing via the edu:// protocol (a clean-by-design network architecture that protects children without relying on reactive parental controls).
  • 60×60 Electronic Dough (Sphere 2): A real-time 3D simulation of a deformable matrix of 3,600 sensors and potentiometers synchronized with a 2D LED radar. Across 5 real sites (Shackleton Crater, Vallis Schröteri, Rima Hadley, and Mare Tranquillitatis on the Moon, plus Jezero Crater on Mars), the player operates two engineering modes: Rover Bridge (leveling terrain crevasses so an autonomous vehicle can cross) and Anti-Radiation Shield Wall (molding regolith berms around the capsule while balancing RadLab radiation dose reduction against power loss from shadows cast on the solar panels).
  • Habitat Workshop with Real Trade-Offs (Sphere 3): No upgrade is free; choosing 70° Zigzag solar panels, a 3D-printed regolith dome, or a hydroponic bio-garden requires taking on real deployment and energy-consumption costs that shape the rest of the mission.
  • 3-Sol Mission Simulator (Sphere 4): Management of competing resources (Power, Life Support, and Health/Shielding) against real solar flares pulled from NASA DONKI, biological wear documented in NASA OSDR, and Earth–Mars communication delays, culminating in the issuance of an Official Diploma.
  • Orbit and Docking Simulator (Sphere 5): An approach maneuver using RCS thrusters, Clohessy-Wiltshire orbital physics, and an acoustic proximity sonar until achieving a Hard Dock with the orbital station.

What benefits and impact does it have? It bridges the gap between abstract space outreach and active learning: students understand why every decision in a space mission carries a cumulative cost over time. By integrating the clean edu:// environment and being lightweight, free, and voice-guided, it is built for classrooms, science clubs, museums, and school environments with limited connectivity.

Tools, languages, and software used:

  • Frontend & 3D Rendering: HTML5, CSS3 (Tailwind CSS), JavaScript (ES6+), Three.js (r128 WebGL with InstancedMesh for 3,600 simultaneous channels), and HTML5 Canvas 2D.
  • Audio & Accessibility: Web Speech API (SpeechSynthesis prioritizing Argentine Spanish es-AR voice) and Web Audio API (procedural synthesis for orbital sonar and tactile feedback).
  • Scientific Integration: NASA Open APIs (DONKI via asynchronous fetch with a verifiable offline archived dataset as fallback), NASA RadLab dosimetry parameters, NASA OSDR space biology, NASA Mars Trek / LRO topography, and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) hydroponics guidelines.
  • Browser Compatibility (Note for Judges/Evaluators): For an optimal experience with 3D WebGL acceleration (3,600 sensors) and neural Argentine Spanish (es-AR) voice synthesis, opening the simulator in Microsoft Edge or Google Chrome is recommended. (In browsers like Brave, Brave Shields must be disabled to enable the Speech API and 2D radar readout).

Creativity and factors considered by the team: We translated the physical-tactile concept of a remote-sensing sensor matrix into a digital topographic sculpting tool where the player "molds" lunar and Martian terrain to protect their crew. We prioritized three core resources to avoid overwhelming 7–12-year-old players, eliminated "cost-free safe" choices, designed the experience under edu:// child-safety principles, and added an on-screen Scientific Traceability panel so students and judges can verify the real NASA and CSA sources.

Artificial Intelligence (AI / IS) Transparency Statement: AI assistance tools were used to accelerate JavaScript/Three.js code structuring and pedagogical copywriting; conceptual design, game mechanics, scientific data integration, and final validation were carried out entirely by our team without using NASA trademarks or logos.
